claim: Difficulty achieving complete, specific, and homogenous staining is a major bottleneck preventing the widespread use of tissue clearing techniques to image large volumes of human tissue.
source: Difficulty achieving complete, specific, and homogenous staining is a major bottleneck preventing the widespread use of tissue clearing techniques to image large volumes of human tissue.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the abstract and is supported by the subsequent methodology developed to address it.

claim: Results from a library of mouse tissue correlate well with results from a similarly prepared library of human brain tissue.
source: Results from a library of mouse tissue correlate well with results from a similarly prepared library of human brain tissue, suggesting mouse tissue is an adequate substitute for protocol optimization.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing mouse and human tissue staining results presented in Figure 7.

claim: Mouse tissue is an adequate substitute for protocol optimization for human tissue.
source: Results from a library of mouse tissue correlate well with results from a similarly prepared library of human brain tissue, suggesting mouse tissue is an adequate substitute for protocol optimization.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data between mouse and human tissue results.

claim: Procedural differences do not influence every antibody-antigen pair in the same way.
source: These data show that procedural differences do not influence every antibody-antigen pair in the same way, and minor changes can have deleterious effects, therefore, optimization should be conducted for each target.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing different antibodies respond differently to the same protocol changes (Figures 3-7).

claim: Minor changes in IHC protocols can have deleterious effects on antibody staining.
source: These data show that procedural differences do not influence every antibody-antigen pair in the same way, and minor changes can have deleterious effects, therefore, optimization should be conducted for each target.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing protocol variations affecting staining quality.

claim: Optimization should be conducted for each target antibody.
source: These data show that procedural differences do not influence every antibody-antigen pair in the same way, and minor changes can have deleterious effects, therefore, optimization should be conducted for each target.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed variability in antibody responses to different protocols.

claim: Tissue clearing involves lipid removal and refractive index matching to significantly decrease light scattering.
source: One promising method, tissue clearing, involves lipid removal and refractive index matching to significantly decrease light scattering.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tissue clearing techniques.

claim: Tissue clearing allows for light microscopy to observe the distribution of individual molecules throughout entire organs millimeters to centimeters in size.
source: Tissue clearing allows for light microscopy to observe the distribution of individual molecules throughout entire organs millimeters to centimeters in size (Ueda et al., 2020b; Richardson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Complete, specific and homogenous staining is now the most common bottleneck preventing the widespread use of tissue clearing in samples that cannot be modified to express fluorescent proteins such as human tissue.
source: This is rarely the case and complete, specific and homogenous staining is now the most common bottleneck preventing the widespread use of tissue clearing in samples that cannot be modified to express fluorescent proteins such as human tissue.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the field and is supported by the context of the study.

claim: Most tissue clearing methods have been optimized for studies in rodents.
source: Therefore, most tissue clearing methods have been optimized for studies in rodents, and only a few recent studies apply clearing techniques to human tissue (Scardigli et al., 2021; Lai et al., 2018; Susaki et al., 2020; Matos et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature showing limited human tissue studies.

claim: Only a few recent studies apply clearing techniques to human tissue.
source: Therefore, most tissue clearing methods have been optimized for studies in rodents, and only a few recent studies apply clearing techniques to human tissue (Scardigli et al., 2021; Lai et al., 2018; Susaki et al., 2020; Matos et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by specific citations to recent human tissue clearing studies.

claim: Successful IHC requires four fundamentals: (1) the antibody cannot denature, (2) the epitope cannot denature, (3) the antibody must diffuse completely through the tissue, and (4) the antibody must only bind its intended target.
source: Successful IHC requires four fundamentals: (1) the antibody cannot denature, (2) the epitope cannot denature, (3) the antibody must diffuse completely through the tissue, and (4) the antibody must only bind its intended target.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IHC requirements.

claim: Differences in staining quality can result from biological heterogeneity such as small differences in tissue composition, individual antibodies, their epitopes, and overall tissue structure.
source: It is well understood that differences in staining quality can result from biological heterogeneity such as small differences in tissue composition, individual antibodies, their epitopes, and overall tissue structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of IHC.

claim: Variability in IHC can be induced by each step of an IHC protocol.
source: However, further variability can be induced by each step of an IHC protocol (Kim et al., 2016; Matos et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IHC protocols can usually be reproduced with the same tissues, antibodies, and fluorophores.
source: Because of this, IHC protocols can usually be reproduced with the same tissues, antibodies, and fluorophores.
evidence: This is a general observation about IHC reproducibility.

claim: It is common to have difficulties extending IHC protocols to different antibodies or tissues.
source: Unfortunately, it is common to have difficulties extending these protocols to different antibodies or tissues.
evidence: This is a known problem in the field that motivates the study.

claim: Tissue sections 0.5–1.0 mm thick and antibody incubation times of 18–24 hr are sufficient to assess the influence of chosen conditions on IHC staining quality.
source: Through empirical testing, we found tissue sections 0.5–1.0 mm thick and antibody incubation times of 18–24 hr to be sufficient to assess the influence of our chosen conditions on IHC staining quality (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by empirical testing data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The signal when staining 24 hr and under may be limited by the depletion of antibodies on their way through the tissue.
source: It should be noted that these data suggest the signal when staining 24 hr and under may be limited by the depletion of antibodies on their way through the tissue, which should be considered when making comparisons of staining quality.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on antibody incubation times.

claim: Increasing delipidation time to 2 days had a positive influence on NeuN staining.
source: Increasing delipidation time to 2 days had a positive influence on NeuN staining, and no influence on Glut1 staining, but both showed worse IHC when increasing the delipidation time further.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different delipidation times.

claim: Increasing delipidation time to 2 days had no influence on Glut1 staining.
source: Increasing delipidation time to 2 days had a positive influence on NeuN staining, and no influence on Glut1 staining, but both showed worse IHC when increasing the delipidation time further.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different delipidation times.

claim: Both NeuN and Glut1 showed worse IHC when increasing the delipidation time beyond 2 days.
source: Increasing delipidation time to 2 days had a positive influence on NeuN staining, and no influence on Glut1 staining, but both showed worse IHC when increasing the delipidation time further.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different delipidation times.

claim: Incubation of tissue at 50°C for 1 hr prior to antibody incubation improved staining for Glut1 and NeuN.
source: Incubation of tissue at 50°C for 1 hr prior to antibody incubation improved staining for Glut1 and NeuN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data testing different pre-treatment conditions.

claim: Glycine treatment had no significant effect on NeuN staining.
source: Glycine treatment had no significant effect on NeuN staining, but inhibited Glut1 staining.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data testing glycine treatment.

claim: Glycine treatment inhibited Glut1 staining.
source: Glycine treatment had no significant effect on NeuN staining, but inhibited Glut1 staining.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data testing glycine treatment.

claim: Incubating antibodies at room temperature improved NeuN staining and Glut1 staining.
source: Incubating antibodies at room temperature improved NeuN staining and on Glut1 staining.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different incubation temperatures.

claim: Staining with DAPI appears insensitive to the different protocols tested.
source: Intriguingly, staining with DAPI appears insensitive to the different protocols (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inclusion of PFA in the hydrogel resulted in decreased IHC quality for both Glut1 and NeuN.
source: Inclusion of PFA in the hydrogel resulted in decreased IHC quality for both Glut1 and NeuN, however this significantly improved IHC of dopamine receptor 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing protocols with and without PFA in hydrogel.

claim: Inclusion of PFA in the hydrogel significantly improved IHC of dopamine receptor 2.
source: Inclusion of PFA in the hydrogel resulted in decreased IHC quality for both Glut1 and NeuN, however this significantly improved IHC of dopamine receptor 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The optimal protocol for simultaneously staining Glut1, NeuN, and DAPI is to delipidate for 2 days, place the tissue at 50°C for 1 hr before incubating with antibodies, and incubating the antibodies at room temperature.
source: Therefore, we ascertained the optimal protocol for simultaneously staining Glut1, NeuN, and DAPI was to delipidate for 2 days, place the tissue at 50°C for 1 hr before incubating with antibodies, and incubating the antibodies at room temperature.
evidence: This is determined from the experimental data comparing different protocol conditions.

claim: The optimal conditions for Glut1, NeuN, and DAPI would result in no staining of dopamine receptor 2.
source: Importantly, these same conditions would result in no staining of dopamine receptor 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different conditions can have opposite effects on the quality of staining and depth of antibody penetration.
source: Together, these results show that different conditions can have opposite effects on the quality of staining and depth of antibody penetration and reinforce the importance of optimizing sample preparation conditions for each antibody.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing variable effects of different conditions.

claim: The trends in staining quality are similar for both monoclonal and polyclonal GFAP antibodies across all conditions.
source: Immunolabeling GFAP with different antibodies shows that the trends in staining quality are similar for both antibodies across all conditions (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing two different GFAP antibodies shown in Figure 5.

claim: Conditions that enhance GFAP stability and prevent denaturation of its epitopes have a positive effect on all GFAP antibodies provided the antibodies are of high quality, have high specificity and limited off-target binding.
source: This suggests that conditions that enhance GFAP stability and prevent denaturation of its epitopes have a positive effect on all GFAP antibodies provided the antibodies are of high quality, have high specificity and limited off-target binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar trends observed for different GFAP antibodies.

claim: IHC of GFAP with the tested antibodies is limited more by denaturation of the epitope than the antibody itself.
source: This also suggests that IHC of GFAP with these antibodies is limited more by denaturation of the epitope than the antibody itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different antibodies show similar responses to protocol changes.

claim: It is recommended to use primary antibodies directly conjugated to fluorophores whenever possible.
source: As this approach also reduces the length of the staining protocol, it is recommended to use primary antibodies directly conjugated to fluorophores whenever possible.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the advantages observed in the study.

claim: There was significantly more variability between tau antibodies than seen with GFAP antibodies.
source: There was significantly more variability between tau antibodies than seen with GFAP antibodies, primarily due to the inability for DAKO total tau antibody to effectively penetrate beyond the tissue's surface (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different tau antibodies shown in Figure 6.

claim: DAKO total tau antibody was unable to effectively penetrate beyond the tissue's surface.
source: There was significantly more variability between tau antibodies than seen with GFAP antibodies, primarily due to the inability for DAKO total tau antibody to effectively penetrate beyond the tissue's surface (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: All three tau antibodies (AT8, HT7, and DAKO) labeled similar structures when used in traditional IHC in microtome slices of human tissue.
source: Importantly, when used in traditional IHC in microtome slices of human tissue, all three of these antibodies labeled similar structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar trends in optimal IHC protocols were observed for AT8 and HT7 anti-tau antibodies in mouse tissue expressing human tau.
source: As expected, similar trends in optimal IHC protocols were observed for AT8 and HT7 anti-tau antibodies in mouse tissue expressing human tau (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and showed no labeling in a negative control; mice without tau expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: AT8 and HT7 anti-tau antibodies showed no labeling in mice without tau expression.
source: As expected, similar trends in optimal IHC protocols were observed for AT8 and HT7 anti-tau antibodies in mouse tissue expressing human tau (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and showed no labeling in a negative control; mice without tau expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Testing of IHC protocols for NeuN and Glut1 in human tissue showed similar changes in staining quality and depth when compared to mouse tissue.
source: Surprisingly, our testing of IHC protocols for NeuN and Glut1 in human tissue showed similar changes in staining quality and depth when compared to mouse tissue (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mouse and human tissue shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both human and mouse tissue showed decreases in staining quality with increasing clearing time and fixation with PFA.
source: Both human and mouse tissue showed decreases in staining quality with increasing clearing time and fixation with PFA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different clearing and fixation conditions.

claim: Room temperature antibody incubation improved Glut1 and NeuN staining in both mouse and human tissue.
source: Room temperature antibody incubation as well as epitope unmasking at 50°C for 1 hr prior to antibody incubation improved Glut1 and NeuN staining in both mouse and human tissue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different incubation conditions in both species.

claim: Epitope unmasking at 50°C for 1 hr prior to antibody incubation improved Glut1 and NeuN staining in both mouse and human tissue.
source: Room temperature antibody incubation as well as epitope unmasking at 50°C for 1 hr prior to antibody incubation improved Glut1 and NeuN staining in both mouse and human tissue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different pre-treatment conditions in both species.

claim: The NeuN antibody appears to accumulate off-target in human tissue, which is not observed in mouse tissue.
source: It is also worth noting that this NeuN antibody appears to accumulate off-target in the human tissue, which is not observed in the mouse tissue.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data comparing mouse and human tissue staining.

claim: Complete penetration and simultaneous labeling of 1 mm thick human tissue with NeuN, Glut1, and AT8 antibodies was achieved by following the optimal IHC protocol.
source: By carefully following the optimal IHC protocol determined in this work, we were able to achieve complete penetration and simultaneous labeling of the 1 mm thick human tissue with all three antibodies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The Glut1-labeled vasculature and AT8-labeled tau are extremely well defined and could be easily quantitated in the optimized protocol.
source: Both the Glut1-labeled vasculature and AT8-labeled tau are extremely well defined and could be easily quantitated.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Small changes to an IHC protocol can have profound effects on labeling efficiency.
source: Here, we have found that small changes to an IHC protocol can have profound effects on labeling efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing variable effects of protocol changes.

claim: Poor staining is most often due to denaturation or blockage of the epitope rather than the antibody.
source: Rather than the antibody, our data suggests that poor staining is most often due to denaturation or blockage of the epitope.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar responses for different antibodies against the same target.

claim: The optimal protocols for IHC should be determined for each individual target.
source: These procedural differences do not influence every antibody-antigen pair in the same way, so the optimal protocols for IHC should be determined for each individual target.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed variability in antibody responses to different protocols.

claim: Using combinations of antibodies in the same tissue may require using a protocol with conditions that are acceptable for all antibodies, rather than conditions that are optimal for each individual antibody.
source: Using combinations of antibodies in the same tissue may require using a protocol with conditions that are acceptable for all antibodies, rather than conditions that are optimal for each individual antibody.
evidence: This is a practical consideration derived from the experimental findings.

claim: Temperature, fixation conditions, and other investigated conditions have greater influence the larger the tissue volume becomes.
source: Importantly, temperature, fixation conditions, and the other conditions investigated here have greater influence, the larger the tissue volume becomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that differences are more apparent at depth than at the surface.

claim: The use of tissue sections that are too thin does not allow for appropriate optimization of IHC protocols for thick tissue.
source: For many of the tested protocols, the difference in staining is not apparent at the surface which suggests that the use of tissue sections that are too thin does not allow for appropriate optimization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protocol differences are more apparent at depth.

claim: Mouse tissue is a good model system for determining large-volume IHC protocols for human samples.
source: Most surprising to us was that mouse tissue is a good model system for determining large-volume IHC protocols for human samples.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation data between mouse and human tissue results.

claim: It is important that tissue preparations are identical when using mouse tissue as a model for human tissue.
source: However, these results show that minor procedural changes can disrupt the quality of staining, so it is important that tissue preparations are identical.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed sensitivity to protocol variations.

claim: IHC protocols in large-volume tissue that requires clearing can take weeks or months to complete depending on the initial state and size of the tissue.
source: IHC protocols in large-volume tissue that requires clearing can take weeks or months to complete depending on the initial state and size of the tissue (Susaki et al., 2020; Ueda et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The requirement for human tissue to be processed longer than comparable-sized rodent tissue is not due to intrinsic differences between human and mouse brain tissue, but rather a result of differences in the state of the tissue when clearing experiments are started.
source: Our results suggest that this is not due to intrinsic differences between human and mouse brain tissue, but rather a result of differences in the state of the tissue when clearing experiments are started.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar responses in mouse and human tissue when prepared identically.

claim: Human tissue is often stored in fixative for extended periods of time.
source: Human tissue is often stored in fixative for extended periods of time and, as our data shows, even a small increase in PFA exposure can have significant influence on IHC quality and depth.
evidence: This is a known practice in the field and is supported by the experimental data showing effects of PFA exposure.

claim: Even a small increase in PFA exposure can have significant influence on IHC quality and depth.
source: Human tissue is often stored in fixative for extended periods of time and, as our data shows, even a small increase in PFA exposure can have significant influence on IHC quality and depth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different PFA exposure conditions.

claim: Tissue that was delipidated for 3 days showed less rapid IHC penetration than tissue that was cleared for 2 days in all cases except for DAPI labeling.
source: To our surprise, tissue that was delipidated for 3 days showed less rapid IHC penetration than tissue that was cleared for 2 days in all cases except for DAPI labeling.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different delipidation times.

claim: Samples can quickly become over-cleared and lose antigenicity.
source: This suggests that samples can quickly become over-cleared and lose antigenicity which may extend the amount of time previously reported as necessary for IHC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that longer clearing times reduced staining quality.

claim: Optimal IHC conditions can be determined for new antibodies within a few days using the described methodology.
source: Then, optimal IHC conditions are determined for new antibodies within a few days (approximately 24 hr for staining, 24 hr for rinsing, 12–24 hr for refractive index matching/clearing, 3 hr to image the samples, and a similar amount of time to quantify and compare the staining quality).
evidence: This is a description of the timeline for the methodology developed in the study.

claim: Tau is a microtubule associated protein that is primarily expressed by neurons and is the main component of neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Tau is a microtubule associated protein that is primarily expressed by neurons and is the main component of neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau protein.

claim: Three days of antibody incubation is sufficient for consistent and thorough staining across brain regions in 500 µm mouse tissue.
source: It should be noted that we found 3 days of antibody incubation sufficient for consistent and thorough staining across brain regions in 500 µm mouse tissue (Figure 3—figure supplements 8 and 9), and there were no notable downsides to leaving the antibody incubating longer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 8 and 9.

claim: There were no notable downsides to leaving the antibody incubating longer than 3 days.
source: It should be noted that we found 3 days of antibody incubation sufficient for consistent and thorough staining across brain regions in 500 µm mouse tissue (Figure 3—figure supplements 8 and 9), and there were no notable downsides to leaving the antibody incubating longer.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The inability of DAKO total tau antibody to penetrate beyond the tissue surface may be an effect of poor penetration and diffusion of the secondary antibody.
source: However, as the DAKO total tau antibody was not directly conjugated to a fluorophore, we cannot exclude the possibility that the inability to image DAKO-stained tau beyond the surface may be an effect of poor penetration and diffusion of the secondary antibody.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible explanation for the observed results.

claim: Conditions that reduce the antigenicity may significantly enhance the apparent penetration rate.
source: It should be noted that simply relying on depth to half-max staining does not separate the issues of free antibody penetration speed through the tissue nor the extent of antibody depletion along the way, and it is possible that conditions that reduce the antigenicity may significantly enhance the apparent penetration rate.
evidence: This is a cautionary note about interpreting the depth to half-max staining metric.

claim: Human tissue was provided by the Massachusetts Alzheimer's Disease Research Center with approval from the Mass General Brigham IRB.
source: Human tissue was provided by the Massachusetts Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC) with approval from the Mass General Brigham IRB (1999P009556).
evidence: This is a statement about the source and ethical approval for human tissue samples.

claim: Three human participants with AD were selected from the Massachusetts Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.
source: Three human participants with AD were selected from the Massachusetts Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.
evidence: This is a description of the human tissue samples used in the study.

claim: C57Bl/6J mice were used for most tissue experiments.
source: Male and female C57Bl/6J mice (Jackson Laboratory 000664) were used for most tissue experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the mouse strains used in the study.

claim: 10- to 12-month-old male hTau mice that express only human tau isoforms were used for tissue to test IHC of tau.
source: For tissue to test IHC of tau, 10- to 12-month-old male hTau mice bred from a local colony (B6.Cg-Mapttm1(EGFP)Klt Tg(MAPT)8cPdav/J, Jackson Laboratory 005491) that express only human tau isoforms were used.
evidence: This is a description of the mouse model used for tau experiments.

claim: hTau knockout mice were used as controls for tau IHC experiments.
source: hTau knockout mice bred from a local colony (Mapttm1(EGFP)Klt/J, Jackson Laboratory 004779) were used as controls for tau IHC experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the control mice used in tau experiments.

claim: Mouse experiments were performed with approval of local institutional review boards (IACUC protocol # 2019N000026).
source: Mouse experiments were performed with approval of local institutional review boards (IACUC protocol # 2019N000026).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for animal experiments.

claim: The baseline protocol involved minimal processing and gentle conditions.
source: The baseline protocol involved minimal processing and gentle conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the baseline protocol used in the study.

claim: The baseline protocol involved tissue fixed in 4% PFA for 2 days post-perfusion, embedded in hydrogel made of 4% acrylamide, delipidated in SDS for 1 day at 37°C, rinsed in PBST at 4°C, and incubated with antibodies at 4°C for 18 hr.
source: Specifically, the tissue was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 2 days post-perfusion, embedded in hydrogel made of 4% acrylamide, delipidated in sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) for 1 day at 37°C, rinsed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) with 0.2% Triton X-100 (PBST) at 4°C, and incubated with antibodies at 4°C for 18 hr.
evidence: This is a detailed description of the baseline protocol.

claim: Conditions including boiling samples in citrate buffer before or after delipidation, heating to temperatures above 70°C before immunolabeling, and removal or decrease of PFA concentration in the transcardial perfusion or post-perfusion fixing step were universally observed to negatively impact IHC or tissue integrity.
source: However, these conditions were universally observed to negatively impact IHC or tissue integrity, so they were excluded from our final library.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations during protocol development.

claim: Mouse and human tissue was stored following delipidation and successfully used up to 6 months later.
source: Additional mouse and human tissue was stored following delipidation, then successfully used up to 6 months later by resuming from the pre-IHC tissue processing state.
evidence: This is a description of tissue storage and viability.

claim: The final concentration of each antibody in solution was 5 µg/ml.
source: The final concentration of each antibody in solution was 5 µg/ml.
evidence: This is a description of the antibody concentration used in the experiments.

claim: Samples were stable stored in RI-matching solution at room temperature and could be re-imaged for at least 3 months.
source: Samples were stable stored in this solution at room temperature and could be re-imaged for at least 3 months.
evidence: This is a description of sample stability after refractive index matching.
